_README: A player-format description for songfmt.py. Copy this, fill it in for your
game, and delete the underscore keys -- they are documentation and are
ignored. `formats/mm-tia.json` is the same file filled in for a real game.
The tool knows nothing about any particular player. Everything specific to
a game lives here, which means writing this file IS the reverse
engineering. The way to do it:
1. `audiotrace.py game.a78` -- finds the audio writes and the tables
feeding them. That gives you addresses, not meaning.
2. Disassemble the routine it points at and read how a note is decoded.
3. Fill this in, `songfmt.py pull`, then `songfmt.py render --verify`
against a capture of the same song. Anything less than 100% means
your reading is wrong somewhere -- which is the point of the check.
An address is written `space:hex`, e.g. `f6:7F65` or `b3:8C3A`, using the
space names the disassembler uses for this cartridge.
name: Some Game -- TIA music player
_match: Optional. Lets a tool find this file for a cartridge on its own, instead
of being told with --format. Leave it out while you are still working the
`player` is the key to prefer: the fingerprint from
`audiotrace.py game.a78 --signature`, which hashes the code around the
cartridge's audio writes. A format file describes an ENGINE, and the
engine is what recurs -- across the library, 40 fingerprints span more
than one game and cover 373 images. Matching on a title finds one game;
matching on the player finds every cartridge built on it.
`title` (substring of the header title) and `size` (ROM bytes) are also
checked when present, and are worth adding if a fingerprint turns out to
be shared by games whose tables are in different places.
A fingerprint says *same engine*, not *same addresses*. A tool that
matches on it and then fails to read should fall back, not stop.
_voices: how many channels the player drives; voice N is channel N
_songs: The top-level table: `count` songs, `stride` bytes apart, each holding a
pointer to a track per voice at the offsets in `voice_ptr`.
`banks` matters on a banked cartridge. A pointer into the paged window is
read against whatever bank was mapped when the song started, so the same
address is two different tunes depending on where it was started from.
Map song number -> bank for any song whose data is not in a fixed bank.
Getting this wrong is silent: you get a plausible song from the wrong
bytes -- so it is left empty here rather than half-filled. On a linear
cartridge, leave it empty for real.
_track: A track is the arrangement: a list of pattern pointers, repeats included.
`end_when` says how the list stops -- `high_byte_zero` means a pointer
whose high byte is 0 ends it, and the low byte is then a command
(loop, stop, chain), kept as `terminator` when `keep_terminator` is set.
`limit` is a safety stop, not a format fact.
_pattern: `count_prefixed`: one count byte, then that many fixed-size records.
A pattern owns exactly the bytes it occupies, and songfmt will refuse to
grow one, because whatever follows it belongs to something else.
_note: How one record unpacks. Each field is [byte index, lowest bit, width], so
a field can straddle nothing but sits anywhere inside its byte.
Expect fields to share a byte in ways that look wrong until you see why:
a 5-bit AUDF leaves three bits spare in the pitch byte, and players reuse
them. `rest_when` is the test for a silent note.
_durations: The note's `duration` field indexes this table, giving a length in frames
(one row per frame at 60 Hz NTSC, 50 Hz PAL). Omit if durations are
_waveforms: Optional. If the note's `waveform` field is an INDEX into a table rather
than an AUDC value, describe the table here. Without it, songfmt treats
the field as the register value directly.
_instruments: Optional, and needed only for `songfmt.py render`. Volume over time is a
program, not a layout, so it is not described declaratively: name an
`engine` that songfmt implements and give the byte offsets its rows use.
An engine songfmt does not implement is refused rather than approximated,
because a song rendered with the wrong envelope sounds convincing and is
adsr5 -- five stages (attack, decay, sustain, release, off), one step
per frame. Volume is an 8-bit accumulator whose high nibble
reaches a 4-bit volume register, so decrements smaller than $10
are slopes. The sustain stage writes no volume at all. Needs
these `fields`: flags, counter, peak, attack, decay_len,
If your player's envelope is not one of these, leave this out: pull and
push still work, and only `render` is unavailable.
